questions.prompt: During pre-study physiologic calibration, the patient follows the eye-movement instructions. One EOG channel remains nearly flat, but the other EOG channel shows eye movement and the EEG channels appear intact. What is the best next action before lights out?
options: Repeat the eye-movement commands and start the study if the other EOG channel still responds
Check the affected EOG electrode, connector, impedance and derivation; restore the signal and repeat calibration
Use the functioning EOG derivation as a substitute for both EOG channels without documenting a limitation
Increase display gain on the flat EOG channel and accept calibration without checking signal integrity
questions.answer: Check the affected EOG electrode, connector, impedance and derivation; restore the signal and repeat calibration
questions.rationale: The patient performed the eye-movement maneuver and the other EOG channel responds, so the near-flat trace warrants a channel-specific technical check. Inspect the affected electrode, connector, impedance and derivation, correct the signal path, and repeat/annotate the physiologic calibration before lights out. Display gain or another functioning channel alone does not establish that the affected derivation is recording correctly. This is a signal-quality decision, not a sleep-stage interpretation.

questions.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.prompt: A 12-year-old has a PSG before a planned MSLT. The recording provides eight hours in bed but only six hours and twenty minutes of sleep. What should the technologist do?
options: Proceed because the required eight hours in bed was provided, even though total sleep time is under seven hours
Proceed because six hours of total sleep time meets the minimum stated for adult MSLT preparation
Flag the short sleep time and communicate with the ordering team under the laboratory's protocol before proceeding
Extend the first daytime nap trial to make up for the forty minutes of insufficient overnight sleep
questions.answer: Flag the short sleep time and communicate with the ordering team under the laboratory's protocol before proceeding
questions.rationale: The AASM pediatric MSLT protocol calls for an attended preceding PSG allowing at least eight hours in bed and at least seven hours of total sleep time. This 12-year-old obtained only six hours and twenty minutes of sleep, so meeting the time-in-bed target alone does not meet the pediatric sleep requirement. The adult six-hour sleep minimum must not be substituted, and daytime nap duration cannot replace insufficient overnight sleep. The technologist should document the discrepancy and obtain clinician/protocol direction rather than unilaterally treating the study as valid.

questions.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.prompt: An adult is scheduled for MSLT immediately after a split-night study in which PAP pressures were adjusted. Which response best protects test validity?
options: Proceed because six hours of total sleep on the PSG is sufficient even when PAP pressures were adjusted
Recognize that an MSLT should not follow a PAP-adjustment night and contact the ordering team about rescheduling or further direction
Proceed if respiratory events were adequately controlled at the final PAP pressure during the treatment portion
Proceed because the MSLT was scheduled before the study was converted to a split-night PAP titration
questions.answer: Recognize that an MSLT should not follow a PAP-adjustment night and contact the ordering team about rescheduling or further direction
questions.rationale: The AASM adult MSLT protocol specifies that MSLT should not follow a night when PAP pressures were adjusted, including a split-night or initial PAP titration study. Adequate total sleep time, apparent control of respiratory events at the final pressure, or prior scheduling does not remove this protocol exclusion. Document the circumstances and contact the ordering team for clinician-directed next steps. Do not apply the distinct pediatric minimum sleep requirements to this adult case.

questions.prompt: A nine-year-old child's PSG is found to have respiratory events scored using the adult template solely because the software defaulted to adult criteria. Which correction should the quality reviewer request?
options: Accept the adult respiratory scores if the software's event detections were visually checked
Review and, where necessary, re-score the respiratory events under the AASM pediatric rules applicable to this age, documenting the correction
Update the patient's age in the software without revisiting respiratory events scored under adult criteria
Retain the adult event labels and note the software default in the final technical report
questions.answer: Review and, where necessary, re-score the respiratory events under the AASM pediatric rules applicable to this age, documenting the correction
questions.rationale: The AASM Version 3 public respiratory-scoring FAQ describes adult respiratory criteria as optional for children aged 13 years or older; this nine-year-old is below that option's age boundary. Software defaults and a retrospective notation cannot substitute for review under the age-appropriate pediatric respiratory rules. The reviewer should identify affected epochs, arrange correction as indicated, and document the re-scoring. This rationale is an age-boundary preflight only: the complete applicable licensed AASM Version 3 pediatric respiratory rules and current errata still require direct verification before publication.

questions.prompt: During a diagnostic PSG, nasal-pressure airflow was unavailable from 02:10 to 03:00 because of a disconnected cannula; the channel was restored at 03:00. Which handoff entry best preserves the quality of the recording?
options: Record only that the nasal cannula was reconnected at 03:00 because the signal had recovered
Nasal-pressure signal absent from 02:10–03:00; cause, correction and restoration time recorded, with affected data-quality limitations identified
Describe the overall study as technically limited without specifying the missing channel or its interruption interval
Record zero respiratory events during the interrupted interval because nasal-pressure airflow is unavailable
questions.answer: Nasal-pressure signal absent from 02:10–03:00; cause, correction and restoration time recorded, with affected data-quality limitations identified
questions.rationale: A complete PSG technical log should chronologically identify the missing nasal-pressure signal, the 02:10–03:00 interval, the disconnection, corrective action and signal restoration, and the resulting limitation for later scoring or interpretation. Return of the channel does not erase the gap. Loss of one airflow signal cannot be equated to an absence of respiratory events; other recorded channels must be reviewed using the applicable scoring rules. This question tests technical documentation rather than diagnosis or final respiratory scoring.
